cards.title: Google Ads is a demand-capture channel, not a fix for broken marketing
cards.summary: Treat Google Ads as a demand-capture engine that channels existing purchase intent, not as a rescue for weak product-market fit.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to launch or scale Google Ads for your store versus fixing offer, product and messaging first.
steps: Audit whether you already have a converting offer, an angle and messaging that works — the source recommends proving this on Meta first before scaling on Google.
Reframe Google's role: Meta/TikTok create demand, Google captures it, and email/SMS/backend flows retain customers and lift LTV.
Check your channel mix: the source sees Google as ideally about 20-30% of ecommerce revenue, with Google over-performing beyond that signalling other channels are underperforming.
Before spending, verify your landing pages convert; strong ads with poor pages only drive wasted spend.
Only scale Google once the offer, page and messaging are proven, because Google's comparative search results will expose any weakness.
caveats: The 20-30% revenue figure is the source's heuristic, not a universal benchmark; some stores legitimately exceed it.
This is the presenter's opinion; stores with no proven offer should prioritize offer and page testing before Google scaling.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Treat Google as four ad platforms in one
cards.summary: Plan Google as four distinct placements — search, shopping, YouTube and display — each covering a different intent level.
cards.use_when: Structuring a store's full Google Ads account and deciding which campaign types to build.
steps: Map Search to high-intent and problem-aware queries, from product-level searches down to vague problem searches.
Recognize Shopping as the highest-converting placement — the source reports it can be 60-80% of ecommerce Google ad revenue because image, title, price, offer and reviews appear together.
Use YouTube (including Shorts) for demand generation and top-of-funnel reach, not just direct response.
Reserve Display for remarketing first and cold reach only once you're spending tens of thousands per day.
For most brands, the source recommends focusing only on search, shopping and YouTube until the core is built out.
caveats: The 60-80% shopping share and tens-of-thousands-per-day display threshold are the source's stated heuristics, not universal figures.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Build a cold-customer magnet funnel across Google
cards.summary: Assemble top, middle and bottom-of-funnel Google campaigns so every awareness stage leads to a purchase path.
cards.use_when: Designing the full campaign architecture for an ecommerce store that wants to capture cold customers across Google.
steps: Top of funnel: run YouTube ads (Short), in-stream video and Google Display to generate attention and demand.
Route top-of-funnel traffic to advertorials, listicles, VSLs or quiz funnels before the product page.
Middle of funnel: use prospecting Search, Performance Max (search, shopping, discovery, display) and prospecting Shopping to capture existing demand.
Bottom of funnel: run Branded Search, Branded Shopping and dynamic remarketing targeting homepage and product page visitors.
Tie it together: visitors who drop off at add-to-cart get dynamically remarketed to the homepage or product page.
Name the result honestly: the source claims this combined setup yields a 3-5x return per dollar, but treat this as an example, not a guarantee.
caveats: The 3-5x return is the source's claim from their own client accounts, not a promise for your store.
Funnel pages such as quizzes and advertorials add build effort; the source does not specify minimum traffic to justify them.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Scale at break-even using LTV-to-CAC, not front-end ROAS
cards.summary: Focus on break-even new-customer ROAS/CPA and lifetime value rather than chasing isolated high front-end ROAS.
cards.use_when: Setting bid targets and budgets for a store deciding how aggressively to acquire customers.
steps: Calculate your break-even new-customer ROAS and break-even new-customer CPA so you know the ceiling you can spend per acquisition.
The source's core philosophy: scale ad spend until acquisition is break-even or slightly profitable on first purchase, then capture profit on repeat purchases.
Instead of only pushing CAC down, raise AOV on the first order and lift LTV via email/SMS, remarketing and new product releases.
If LTV is 3-5x, the source argues you can afford to spend 2-3x more to acquire the same customer while keeping the ratio intact.
Judge performance on blended marketing efficiency (total revenue vs total ad spend) rather than individual campaign ROAS alone.
The source states the advertiser who can spend the most to win a customer wins — enabled by a stronger backend, not just bigger budgets.
caveats: This is the presenter's stated scaling philosophy and their opinion on how to win auctions; not a rule for every store.
An LTV-based strategy assumes you have reliable cohort and backend data; otherwise it risks unprofitable spend.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Structure branded traffic separately before scaling
cards.summary: Isolate Branded Search and Branded Shopping from prospecting so Google doesn't waste budget converting people who already know you.
cards.use_when: Cleaning up campaign segmentation in a Google Ads account before increasing spend.
steps: Create a dedicated Branded Search campaign with absolute impression-share targeting to protect your brand terms and block competitor bids.
Create a separate Branded Shopping campaign distinct from your prospecting shopping.
Keep the rest of your budget (the source says 80-90%) on cold traffic, so branded terms don't soak up spend that was already going to convert.
Split prospecting from retargeting campaigns, and split branded from non-branded, so spend is directed at cold customers rather than easy conversions.
Watch for the distortion effect: if branded terms sit in prospecting campaigns, Google will spend on the easiest converters and starve the cold terms where new customers are.
caveats: The 80-90% cold-traffic split and absolute targeting are the source's recommendations; the right split varies by brand.
The source says competitor brand bidding is generally a waste because well-protected brands neutralize it.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: The cold customer magnet funnel structure
cards.summary: A three-layer Google setup — demand generation, demand capture, conversion — covering all awareness stages.
cards.use_when: Designing the full Google campaign architecture for an ecommerce store.
steps: Top of funnel (demand generation): YouTube ads (shorts and in-stream), non-brand search, display; use advertorials, listicles, VSLs or quiz funnels as landing pages.
Middle of funnel (demand capture): Performance Max, Standard Shopping, and Dynamic Search Ads to show products where demand already exists — this is where most ecommerce revenue comes from.
Bottom of funnel (conversion): Branded Search, Branded Shopping and Dynamic Remarketing in Merchant Center to convert high-intent visitors and maximize revenue.
Connect the layers: add-to-cart drop-offs are dynamically retargeted back to homepage or product page; brand-aware users get routed through branded search/shopping.
Verify the structure matches your current stage — brands relying only on a single campaign type will remain vulnerable to competitors.
caveats: The claimed 3-5x return applies to the source's example accounts, not a guaranteed outcome.
Fully building out this system takes roughly 1-4 months per the source; it is not an overnight setup.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Know the role of each ecommerce Google campaign type
cards.summary: Assign campaign types to specific jobs — PMax and Shopping for capture, search for intent, YouTube for demand generation.
cards.use_when: Choosing which campaign types to launch for a store at its current scale and deciding which to prioritize.
steps: Performance Max should be your biggest spender, combined with Standard Shopping to cover the shopping placement and win first-position auctions in your category.
Non-brand search targets high-intent queries plus problem statements and investment statements.
Branded search and branded shopping capture already-aware users cheaply and stop competitors bidding on your terms.
YouTube sits at the top of funnel to generate search volume and can run its own funnel simultaneously.
Dynamic remarketing ties it all together, re-targeting anyone who visited your homepage, product page or add-to-cart.
Only add YouTube and cold search campaigns once branded search, shopping and Performance Max are established.
caveats: The source warns Performance Max is black-box and must be controlled properly to avoid wasted spend.
Recommended ordering assumes a baseline of conversion data already exists.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: The three phases of ecommerce Google Ads growth
cards.summary: Sequence Google Ads growth — foundation/testing, then bidding and expansion, then scale — rather than launching everything at once.
cards.use_when: Deciding what to build first when launching or rebuilding a store's Google Ads account.
steps: Phase 1 (30-60 days): launch branded search, branded shopping and prospecting shopping; set up conversion tracking and analytics; use manual bidding to control spend while waiting for at least one conversion per day over 30 days.

Phase 2 (roughly months 2-6): shift to max conversions or tROAS based on margins and break-even ROAS; remove low-performing keywords; add retargeting and audience segmentation; launch YouTube and Performance Max.
Phase 3 (after ~6 months): increase budget on high-performing campaigns; expand to new search/shopping keywords using collected data; use Performance Max to scale with control.
Once the core is mature, add cold search and display if you have extra spend to build out the account fully.
Expect full build-out of a Google system covering ~90% of the inventory you'd bid on to take roughly 1-4 months.
caveats: The 30-60 day, 2-6 month and 6-month windows are the source's heuristics, not fixed rules.
Manual bidding in phase 1 assumes you can monitor and adjust spend regularly.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Trust Google's automation but set guardrails
cards.summary: Let Google optimize broadly while controlling the points that matter, rather than micromanaging or abandoning control.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much manual control to keep over keywords, bidding and targeting in a store's Google Ads account.
steps: Let the creative do the targeting: go broad on keywords and audiences, and avoid over-restricting to preset signals so Google can find new converting terms.
For standard shopping and branded search, keep tighter control — the source recommends absolute impression-share targeting on brand search.
Use automated bidding (tROAS/tCPA) only on campaigns where it makes sense, since Google bids in real time more efficiently than manual for those.
Set clear constraints: run negative keyword scripts to filter low-intent searches, and manually prune via search term reports daily.
Turn off Google's automated recommendations, and scale based on your own performance data, not Google's suggestions to spend more.
Where engagement metrics are weak (high bounce, low session duration), fix the landing page — Google can't fix bad conversion rates.
caveats: The default-to-automation advice is the source's opinion; some accounts may need more manual control.
Negative keyword automation still needs manual review of search terms.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Scale as a process, not an event
cards.summary: Scale spend in steps with daily, weekly and monthly routines that maintain efficiency before adding budget.
cards.use_when: Managing an existing store's Google Ads account and deciding when and how much to increase spend.
steps: Daily: review search terms and add negative keywords; monitor impression share and adjust bids toward the source's 50-60% impression-share target.

Weekly: scale winning campaigns against your break-even ROAS/CPA KPIs; optimize landing pages based on session duration and conversion performance; A/B test new ad copy and landing pages; do Weekly Merchant Center optimizations.
Monthly: increase budgets only if new-customer acquisition and blended ROAS are stable; run a full account review to catch disapprovals or gaps missed during daily/weekly work.
After each increase, confirm KPIs stay stable at the higher spend before scaling further.
If performance declines, fix the leak before increasing budget — the source stresses that scaling is about spending better, not just more.
caveats: The 50-60% impression-share target is the source's stated sweet spot, not a universal benchmark.
Session duration and conversion metrics should be read together, not as standalone signals.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Cut poor SKUs and cap brand spend for efficiency
cards.summary: Improve Google Ads efficiency by concentrating on hero products and limiting branded campaign spend to a small share of budget.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a store's product-level ad spend and branded campaign budgets to eliminate waste.
steps: Identify your hero product — the 80/20 product driving most Google revenue — and concentrate spend there.
Cut poor-performing SKUs rather than advertising every product; not all SKUs are scalable on Google per the source.
Cap branded campaign spend at a maximum of around 10% of monthly spend; the source prefers 3-8%.
Use tROAS/tCPA bidding to keep spend focused on efficient, converting traffic.
Target the goal of increasing acquisition without increasing waste, reviewing SKU-level and brand-level spend regularly.
caveats: The 10% maximum and 3-8% range are the source's heuristics; overspend thresholds vary by brand maturity and brand-name search volume.
Cutting SKUs should consider whether those products support cross-sell or LTV.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Expand beyond search and shopping with YouTube
cards.summary: Add YouTube and demand-gen campaigns to generate new search volume once native search demand is exhausted.
cards.use_when: Deciding when to move beyond search and shopping campaigns for a store hitting a growth ceiling.
steps: Monitor whether search volume on your product and target queries has gone stagnant.
Introduce YouTube ads (including Shorts) and demand-gen campaigns to expand audience reach beyond the limits of existing search volume.
Use YouTube-generated interest as new intent signals that feed Performance Max and shopping campaigns.
Capture the demand on Google's own channels before competitors bid on it.
The source argues YouTube is currently under-exploited with relatively low CPMs for ecommerce brands, so it's a growth opportunity.
caveats: The low-CPM claim is the source's assertion as of the recording and may not hold over time; verify current auction dynamics.
YouTube as primary demand generation is the source's opinion, not a universal rule for every brand.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Test and iterate ads and landing pages continuously
cards.summary: Run split tests on search ad copy, product feeds and landing pages so you always have a control to beat.
cards.use_when: Setting up ongoing optimization for a store's Google Ads and PDP/landing pages.
steps: A/B test search campaigns and product feeds weekly — new headlines, descriptions and CTAs.
Test landing-page variants too: different layouts and messaging flows, using conversion data to decide.
Keep multiple search ads per ad group as challengers rather than a single control; the goal is to beat the current best.
Automate reporting, bid adjustments and negative keyword scripts to free up time for testing.
The source's reasoning: even a small lift in conversion or CTR can meaningfully increase revenue and let you spend more to acquire customers.
caveats: The source views thinking you have the perfect ad without testing as a mistake; expect to run multiple variants.
Weekly testing cadence is the source's recommendation; test duration should respect statistical significance.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Make the offer the centerpiece of Google ads
cards.summary: Since Google shows your ad next to competitors, a stronger offer — shipping, BOGO, bundles — drives the click and conversion.
cards.use_when: Designing ad copy and promotions for a store competing in comparative Google search and shopping results.
steps: Because Google is a comparative shopping platform, decide what makes your offer visibly better than the alternatives shown alongside you.
Use shipping thresholds and frame free shipping as 'shipping on us' so customers feel they already have it.
Test offers like buy-one-get-one, buy-two-get-one, percentage off, or for high-AOV products (above roughly $100) a dollar amount off like $50 off.
Put the offer everywhere in the ad so it appears in the context shoppers compare.
Consider bundling to differentiate and simultaneously raise AOV, which gives more margin to advertise.
caveats: The above-$100 AOV suggestion and 'shipping on us' framing are the source's tips, not universal rules.
Offer strength must pair with a congruent landing page, or clicks won't convert.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Diagnose weak performance via landing page congruence
cards.summary: When ads get clicks but no conversions, check session duration and ad-page congruence before blaming the ads.
cards.use_when: Troubleshooting a store's Google Ads where impressions and clicks are strong but conversions are low.
steps: Separate the ad's job (get the click) from the landing page's job (make the sale).
Check average session duration as a proxy for whether the page matches what the ad promised.
If people bounce quickly, the page likely isn't relevant to what they clicked for — fix page relevance rather than the ad.
Confirm the offer shown in the ad also appears on the landing page so the shopper's expectation is met.
Only after ruling out page and congruence issues should you treat it as a targeting or ad-copy problem.
caveats: Average session duration is a rough proxy for congruence, not a definitive metric.
The source recommends prioritizing impression share, CPC, CTR, conversion rate and conversion count before session duration.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Prioritize AOV over COGS cuts for scalable unit economics
cards.summary: Improve ad scalability mainly by increasing average order value and leveraging LTV, not by squeezing down COGS.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether a store has the margin to run and scale Google Ads.
steps: Check that you have enough margin to reinvest into advertising; without margin you cannot scale.
Rather than focusing first on lowering COGS, the source argues to raise AOV because it offers more leverage without risking product quality or supplier relationships.
Increase AOV through stronger offers and bundles.
Factor LTV into how much you can afford to pay: a strong LTV may let you go break-even or slightly negative (the source gives a 0.8 example) and recover it over the next 12 months.
Set your break-even new-customer ROAS and CPA from these numbers, then align bids and budgets with them.
caveats: The 0.8 example is illustrative, not a standard; your acceptable first-order loss depends on your own cohort data.
The source's preference for AOV over COGS applies when product quality and supplier terms shouldn't be compromised.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Track the metrics that matter for ecommerce Google Ads
cards.summary: Monitor impression share, CPC, CTR, conversion rate and conversion count, plus average session duration, to steer campaigns.
cards.use_when: Building a reporting dashboard or weekly review for a store's Google Ads account.
steps: Track number of conversions and conversion rate to judge sales impact.
Track CTR and CPC to gauge ad relevance and auction competitiveness.
Prioritize impression share — the source ranks it highest because low share correlates with high CPC, low CTR and low conversion rate.
Add average session duration as a sixth metric to measure ad-to-page congruence.
Optimize for purchases, not add-to-carts or clicks, in ecommerce Google Ads.
Set these against your break-even new-customer ROAS and CPA to know how much you can bid.
caveats: The source's ordering of metric priority (impression share first) is their opinion, not an established standard.
Optimizing toward purchases assumes sufficient conversion volume; low-volume stores may need interim goals.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx
